entries.name: Elgin Chantrell
entries.text: Estate and acreage country that still feels rural, even inside city limits: that’s Elgin Chantrell. The space is the main attraction, and most of the families I talk to have Chantrell Creek Elementary and Elgin Park Secondary in mind.

entries.name: Grandview Heights
entries.text: Move-up families looking for a newer house tend to land in Grandview Heights. Grandview Heights Secondary and Edgewood Elementary pull a lot of them here, and Highway 99 commuters like having both the border and downtown within easy reach.

entries.name: Greenway
entries.text: At South Ridge Club, the Greenway townhome complex is all about its shared clubhouse. It attracts three groups: families moving up from a condo, downsizers who want the clubhouse lifestyle, and Southridge school families.

entries.name: Hazelmere
entries.text: Hazelmere, which locals also call Hall’s Prairie, is true estate country. Much of the Little Campbell River watershed here is Agricultural Land Reserve farmland, so that open, rural feel is protected.

entries.name: Jacobsen
entries.text: Inside Grandview Heights, Jacobsen offers a townhome option. It’s a good first step into a townhome, especially for families who want the Sunnyside and Grandview Heights Secondary catchments.

entries.name: King George Corridor, South Surrey
entries.text: The King George Corridor appeals to two kinds of buyers. Families tend to aim for the Semiahmoo Town Centre end, while investors keep an eye on the density the Official Community Plan allows along the corridor.

entries.name: Morgan Creek
entries.text: Bigger lots and custom homes on a golf course define Morgan Creek, an established community. Golfers love it, downsizers come here from larger South Surrey houses, and families look at Morgan Elementary, Rosemary Heights Elementary or Southridge.

entries.name: Morgan Crossing
entries.text: Built around a retail village, Morgan Crossing is a condo pocket. It’s popular with first-time buyers, with downsizers selling South Surrey houses, and with investors.

entries.name: Pacific Douglas (Douglas), South Surrey
entries.text: Tucked between the Peace Arch and Pacific Highway crossings, Douglas is border living and Surrey’s southernmost urban neighbourhood. The usual trade-off is quick crossing access against how quiet the interior streets are.

entries.name: South Surrey / White Rock
entries.text: South Surrey and White Rock are all about the water. There’s waterfront on Marine Drive and in Crescent Beach, and the view homes one street back sell on the view alone.

entries.name: Sunnyside Park, South Surrey
entries.text: For established streets instead of newer Grandview Heights, there’s Sunnyside Park. It suits buyers who want the Semiahmoo school side of South Surrey, and anyone who’d like Bakerview Park and Sunnyside Acres nearby.

entries.name: Bear Creek / Green Timbers
entries.text: Think of Bear Creek / Green Timbers as Surrey’s nature escape. Larger lots and mature trees sit right beside Bear Creek Park and the Green Timbers Urban Forest.

entries.name: Bolivar Heights
entries.text: Elevation and views toward City Centre are what people value in Bolivar Heights, a hill neighbourhood. The City Centre Plan calls for a mixed-use neighbourhood centre here, so it’s one to watch.

entries.name: Bridgeview
entries.text: Low, flat and historic, Bridgeview sits on the Fraser River. When buyers look at it, they weigh three things: the Scott Road Station end, the river frontage and the floodplain building rules.

entries.name: Cedar Hills
entries.text: Between Scott Road and Whalley, around 96 Avenue and 128 Street, Cedar Hills is established single-family North Surrey with planned subdivision houses. Cedar Hills Elementary and Robson Park are in the neighbourhood, with L.A. Matheson Secondary and Moffat Memorial Park just southwest on 122 Street. The Cedar Hills shops are right at the corner, so it’s an easy pick for families who want a quiet street close to City Centre.

entries.name: Clayton
entries.text: Clayton ranks among Surrey’s master-planned neighbourhoods. Newer construction, parks and trails, and the Clayton Community Centre are what bring people here.

entries.name: Cloverdale
entries.text: Settled in the mid to late 1800s as a rural farming community, Cloverdale is Surrey’s historic centre. It’s named for the clover that grew in Clover Valley, and you can still feel that history on its streets.

entries.name: East Newton
entries.text: Single-family subdivision houses close to four SD36 schools make East Newton the family end of the Surrey market. Locals call one part of it Chimney Hill.

entries.name: Fleetwood Tynehead
entries.text: Ask Surrey families for a favourite and Fleetwood Tynehead comes up a lot. You get Tynehead Regional Park, schools, shopping along 152 Street and Fraser Highway, and quick Highway 1 access.

entries.name: Fraser Heights
entries.text: Up on a plateau above Highway 1 sits Fraser Heights. Buyers focus on the school cluster around Fraser Heights Secondary and the view lots on the 112 Avenue crest, and they’re often surprised how calm it is with the freeway so close.

entries.name: Guildford
entries.text: Guildford means Guildford Town Centre, Green Timbers and an easy Highway 1 / Port Mann commute across the river.

entries.name: North Surrey
entries.text: North Surrey isn’t really one neighbourhood. It’s Surrey’s urban north, with Whalley, Guildford and Fleetwood pockets around the Green Timbers Urban Forest. People come here for the City Centre towers and Holland Park more than a village feel.

entries.name: Panorama Ridge
entries.text: On Panorama Ridge, the ridge is everything. Buyers weigh half-acre lots, view premiums and south-facing outlooks toward Mud Bay against the smaller lots elsewhere in Newton.

entries.name: Port Kells
entries.text: Port Kells has two sides. North of Highway 1 is a major light-industrial district; south of it is a rural, low-density residential pocket. Either way, highway access is the big selling point.

entries.name: Queen Mary Park, Surrey
entries.text: In central Surrey, park-centred Queen Mary Park is a place where suites are a big part of the appeal. Many detached homes have basement, side or multiple suites, which helps with rental income or a larger household.

entries.name: Royal Heights, Surrey
entries.text: Small and self-contained, Royal Heights is an enclave whose story is elevation and views over the lowland. Most of the houses around the park date from the mid-1960s.

check.suggested: Most of the houses around Royal Heights Park were built in the late 1950s to early 1970s (City of Surrey Corporate Report R017, January 2026).

entries.name: Serpentine
entries.text: Surrey’s equestrian country and rural heart is Serpentine. It’s acreages and horse properties, yet King George Boulevard, Highway 99, South Surrey amenities and the U.S. border are all close.

entries.name: Sullivan Station
entries.text: Families choose Sullivan Station for Sullivan Heights Secondary and the elementary catchments. Larger suburban lots, on streets like 146A Street and toward the Panorama side, add to the appeal.

entries.name: Surrey
entries.text: Surrey is several markets under one name. There are tower condos in Whalley and City Centre, detached houses in Fleetwood, Newton and Panorama Ridge, and low-rise condos in South Surrey. My advice: shop the pocket, not the city.

entries.name: West Newton
entries.text: With RapidBus on both sides, West Newton is a family-house area: the R1 on King George Boulevard by Newton Exchange to the east, and the R6 on Scott Road to the west.

entries.name: Whalley
entries.text: Two markets share the Whalley name: the City Centre condo and townhome core around the SkyTrain stations, and the older detached streets beyond it.

entries.name: Aldergrove
entries.text: Aldergrove has a small-town core around Fraser Highway and 272 Street. Head south toward the U.S. border and it turns rural, with an acreage-edge feel.

entries.name: Brookswood
entries.text: Bigger lots, rural character and family-friendly streets are what Brookswood is known for, with Campbell Valley Park nearby.

entries.name: Campbell Valley
entries.text: Campbell Valley is rural acreage and equestrian country in south Langley, built around Campbell Valley Regional Park and close to the U.S. border.

entries.name: City of Langley
entries.text: People often mix them up, but the City of Langley is its own small city of about 10 square kilometres, separate from the Township around it. Its walkable downtown is the big draw.

entries.name: County Line / Glen Valley
entries.text: Out in Langley’s northeast corner, toward the Abbotsford border, County Line / Glen Valley is farm country on the south shore of the Fraser. It’s some of the prettiest rural land in Langley.

entries.name: Murrayville, Langley
entries.text: Around the historic Five Corners at Fraser Highway and 216 Street, Murrayville is the Township’s traditional civic core and an established central neighbourhood. It’s also one of only two heritage conservation areas in the
flags: one of only two heritage conservation areas

check.note: Township page says Fort Langley and Murrayville are the two areas with heritage designation. 'Only two heritage conservation areas' is not the page's wording. Suggest: 'one of two heritage-designated areas in the Township'.

entries.name: Otter District
entries.text: The rural southeast corner of the Township belongs to Otter District. It runs mostly south of Fraser Highway down to 0 Avenue at the border, centred on the old farm crossroads at 248 Street.

entries.name: Salmon River
entries.text: Named for the river, Salmon River is a rural acreage and farm district. Its Salmon River Uplands designation is there to protect the rural residential character.

entries.name: Walnut Grove
entries.text: Planned since 1979, Walnut Grove is an established planned community in northwest Langley, north of Highway 1. Shops, movie theatres and the Walnut Grove Community Centre make everyday life easy.

check.note: Neighbourhood plan PDF could not be opened for a second check (site blocks readers).

entries.name: Abbotsford
entries.text: Abbotsford is a city of very different pockets: the established Mill Lake and Clearbrook side, Matsqui Prairie farm ground and newer east-side subdivisions. That mix makes sense once you know the city formed in 1995, when Matsqui and Abbotsford joined.

entries.name: Abbotsford East
entries.text: Abbotsford East is the hillside, view side of the city. Established streets along Old Yale Road give way to newer subdivisions on the McKee and Eagle Mountain slopes. In September 2026 it was the city’s largest detached market by listings.

entries.name: Abbotsford West
entries.text: Older houses west of Clearbrook Road and strata homes clustered around South Fraser Way and Sevenoaks give Abbotsford West, the Clearbrook side, its mix. It’s the city’s biggest attached market.

entries.name: Aberdeen
entries.text: Along Bradner Road and Fraser Highway in west Abbotsford, Aberdeen is a rural community. It sits west of Clearbrook and northwest of Abbotsford International Airport.

entries.name: Bradner
entries.text: Surrounded by farmland and partly in the Agricultural Land Reserve, Bradner is a small, historic rural centre on Abbotsford’s west side.

entries.name: Central Abbotsford
entries.text: The heart of the city is Central Abbotsford. Older houses on Mill Lake and Bevan Avenue streets surround the City Centre and Historic Downtown plan areas, and most of Abbotsford’s attached housing is here.

entries.name: Matsqui
entries.text: Flat farm country north of Abbotsford Centre along the Fraser River makes up Matsqui Prairie, with historic Matsqui Village as its rural centre.

entries.name: Poplar, Abbotsford
entries.text: South of Highway 1, Poplar splits in two. The north end has suburban streets around Marshall Road; toward the border, along King Road and Huntingdon Road, it opens up into acreages.

entries.name: Sumas Mountain, Abbotsford
entries.text: Sumas Mountain holds two housing worlds. Lower down are serviced bench subdivisions like Auguston and McKee; higher up is rural acreage on the upper and FVRD roads.

entries.name: Sumas Prairie
entries.text: On the flat former lakebed between Sumas and Vedder Mountains, Sumas Prairie is low-lying farmland between Abbotsford and Chilliwack. Dikes and pump stations protect it from flooding, and I make sure buyers understand that before they buy.

entries.name: Bridal Falls
entries.text: East of Chilliwack, Bridal Falls is a small highway-services community known more for tourist and recreation attractions than city living. It falls under FVRD Electoral Area D, so the City of Chilliwack doesn’t govern it.

entries.name: Chilliwack
entries.text: Chilliwack is a full-service valley city that still runs out to farmland at the edges. There’s the Five Corners and District 1881 downtown, hillside neighbourhoods above the valley floor and ALR fields at the fringe. It’s a good fit if you want city services with a rural backdrop.

check.note: Same document: District 1881 and the heritage shopfront wording are not stated.

entries.name: Chilliwack Downtown
entries.text: Heritage courtyard shops and restaurants have revitalized the historic Five Corners / District 1881 core of downtown Chilliwack.

check.note: City document names Five Corners but mentions District 1881 only in a photo caption; 'heritage courtyard shops' is not stated.

entries.name: Chilliwack Mountain
entries.text: West of downtown and above the valley floor, Chilliwack Mountain is a hillside neighbourhood. People buy here for the elevation and the views.

entries.name: Chilliwack Proper East
entries.text: On the east side of downtown, running out toward Prest Road, Chilliwack Proper East is the older grid. The shops and restaurants of District 1881 are an easy walk or a short drive away. With a mix of older houses and newer builds, it’s for buyers who’d rather be central than out in the subdivisions.

entries.name: Chilliwack Proper South
entries.text: Between Yale Road and Highway 1, around Evans Road, Hocking Avenue and Southlands Crescent, Chilliwack Proper South is the established southern part of the Proper.

entries.name: Chilliwack Proper West
entries.text: Chilliwack Proper West is the older grid west of downtown, around Young Road and Corbould Street. Its older streets and established homes give it real character.

entries.name: Chilliwack River Valley
entries.text: Rural and built around recreation, the Chilliwack River Valley is in FVRD Electoral Area E. People move here for the outdoors, the fishing and the acreage.

entries.name: Columbia Valley
entries.text: South of Cultus Lake lies Columbia Valley, a quiet farming valley that shares FVRD Electoral Area H with Cultus Lake and Lindell Beach. With one main valley road, a handful of farms and acreages, and no road crossing at the U.S. border, it truly feels like the end of the road. It’s for buyers who want land and privacy, with the lake just down the hill.

entries.name: Cultus Lake
entries.text: Mostly second and recreational homes, Cultus Lake is a lake recreation community. It splits between the Cultus Lake Park side at the north end and Lindell Beach at the south.

entries.name: East Chilliwack
entries.text: Acreages, hobby farms and equestrian properties fill East Chilliwack, rural farm country in the Agricultural Land Reserve.

entries.name: Eastern Hillsides, Chilliwack
entries.text: The Eastern Hillsides sit on a bench above the valley floor. Compared with Garrison Crossing and Promontory, you get bigger lots, more privacy and a more rural feel.

entries.name: Fairfield Island
entries.text: By the river, north of Chilliwack Proper, Fairfield Island is a residential area. It appeals to acreage, workshop and custom-home buyers.

entries.name: Garrison Crossing
entries.text: Laid out around Garrison Village and a central boulevard, Garrison Crossing is the redevelopment of the former Canadian Forces Base Chilliwack in Sardis.

entries.name: Greendale
entries.text: Along Sumas Prairie Road, Greendale is rural farm country on the Sumas Prairie side of Chilliwack. Greendale Community Elementary is right in the area, and the Great Blue Heron Nature Reserve on the Vedder River has more than 10 km of trails. People come for acreage, hobby farms and mountain views. Because it’s floodplain farmland, I always have buyers check ALR status and the flood construction level for the exact parcel.

entries.name: Little Mountain
entries.text: Overlooking the Fraser Valley east of downtown Chilliwack, Little Mountain is a hillside view neighbourhood. Don’t confuse it with Chilliwack Mountain, a separate hillside community west of downtown.

entries.name: Popkum
entries.text: Popkum is a small community east of Chilliwack with close ties to the city. Most buyers here want acreage, a rural home or easy highway access.

entries.name: Promontory
entries.text: Above the Vedder/Sardis flats, east of Vedder Road, Promontory is a hillside neighbourhood. It attracts view buyers, families who want the local elementary school and buyers looking for suite income.

entries.name: River Valley
entries.text: River Valley appeals to fishing and recreation buyers, acreage buyers priced out of Chilliwack and Sardis, and full-time residents who commute into the city.

entries.name: Rosedale
entries.text: East of Chilliwack, with the Agricultural Land Reserve setting its limits, Rosedale is a rural village. Typical buyers want acreage or a small farm, or a detached family house in a village setting.

entries.name: Ryder Lake
entries.text: Upland rural country on the slopes around Mount Thom, above Promontory: that’s Ryder Lake. It’s popular with horse and hobby-farm people, view buyers and families who want Sardis schools without living on Sardis streets.

entries.name: Sardis
entries.text: Sardis draws young families chasing G.W. Graham or Sardis Secondary, downsizers coming off Promontory and Ryder Lake acreages, and investors looking at house lots. Garrison Crossing, with its planned streets, Cheam Leisure Centre and Garrison Village, adds to the appeal.

entries.name: Sardis East / Vedder
entries.text: Centred on Sardis Park and Stevenson Road, Sardis East is the part of Sardis east of Vedder Road. Families aim for the Sardis Secondary and Sardis Elementary catchments, and it also suits military families with a Garrison Crossing connection and commuters using the Route 66 stop at Luckakuck Way.

entries.name: Sardis South
entries.text: Sardis South covers the area around Tyson Road, South Sumas Road and Watson Road, roughly between Stevenson Road and Vedder. Families chase the Tyson and Watson school side, and suite and infill buyers look here too.

entries.name: Sardis West Vedder
entries.text: West of Vedder Road, along the Evans Road and Unsworth Road corridors, sits Sardis West Vedder. Families come for the Evans and Unsworth schools, alongside suite-income buyers and downsizers.

entries.name: Vedder Crossing
entries.text: At Vedder Crossing, you’re paying for newer planned streets, river trails, and the UFV and Canada Education Park next door. Buyers include military and RCMP families connected to the old base and training centre, UFV staff and student families, and commuters.

entries.name: Vedder Mountain
entries.text: Vedder Mountain sits between the Vedder River valley floor and the Columbia Valley / Cultus Lake area. Trail riders love having the mountain bike network at the door, and it also suits acreage buyers leaving Sardis and anyone who simply wants out of the subdivisions.

entries.name: West Chilliwack
entries.text: Planned under the Agricultural Area Plan, West Chilliwack is the rural, agricultural west side of the city. Its 55+ buyers tend to be local downsizers, people moving within the Fraser Valley and people relocating from the coast for a better price.

entries.name: Yarrow
entries.text: Outside the City’s Urban Growth Boundary, with ALR land on all sides, Yarrow is a true village. Buyers are often families priced out of Sardis, acreage seekers and people who want Yarrow specifically.

entries.name: Albion
entries.text: Albion, on the east side along Lougheed Highway around 240 Street, is one of Maple Ridge’s big growth pockets. South Albion still has farmland, and the Fraser River runs along the south edge.

entries.name: Cottonwood, Maple Ridge
entries.text: Right against the greenbelt, Cottonwood is a family subdivision. Streets back onto Kanaka Creek Regional Park, Alexander Robinson Elementary on 238B Street sits in the middle of the houses, and Cliff Falls on the Canyon Trail is the local walk.

entries.name: East Central Maple Ridge
entries.text: The downtown side of Maple Ridge is East Central, though locals and the City usually call the west end Downtown, Haney or the Town Centre. Its residential streets run east and north toward 232 Street and 124 Avenue.

entries.name: Maple Ridge
entries.text: Under the Golden Ears, Maple Ridge is a Fraser River city with ten distinct pockets from Albion to Whonnock between the mountains and the river. It works well for commuters on the Lougheed Highway and Dewdney Trunk corridors, and for West Coast Express riders out of Port Haney and Maple Meadows.

entries.name: North Maple Ridge
entries.text: Roughly 224 Street to 240 Street, north of Dewdney Trunk Road and across the Alouette River, North Maple Ridge is the rural north side. It takes in Silver Valley, Yennadon and the acreage ground on the Thornhill side.

entries.name: Northeast Maple Ridge
entries.text: Websters Corners, Whonnock and the Thornhill edge make up Northeast Maple Ridge, the rural east side. Buyers here are weighing acreage, creek frontage and how far they want to be from their neighbours.

entries.name: Northwest Maple Ridge
entries.text: North of Lougheed Highway and Dewdney Trunk Road, from about 224 Street to the Pitt Meadows line, Northwest Maple Ridge covers the west side. Urban streets give way to rural lots as you head north.

entries.name: Silver Valley, Maple Ridge
entries.text: North of the Alouette River, Silver Valley is a newer, mostly detached neighbourhood. It’s a gateway to recreation areas and trail networks, which is a big reason people choose it.

entries.name: Southwest Maple Ridge
entries.text: Hammond is Southwest Maple Ridge, the historic corner bounded by Pitt Meadows and the Katzie First Nation to the west and the Fraser River to the south. Its early-1900s commercial area gives it real character.

check.note: City page does not state the early-1900s commercial area or the boundaries.

entries.name: Thornhill Maple Ridge
entries.text: Heavily forested and mostly residential, Thornhill is a hill with a few farms and nurseries. It’s best known for the big mountain biking and hiking trail network off 256 Street.

entries.name: Websters Corners
entries.text: Just off Dewdney Trunk Road near the Mission border, Websters Corners is rural acreage. There’s mountain biking in the BCIT Woodlot, and the area is an active film-production hub.

entries.name: West Central Maple Ridge
entries.text: Taking in Port Haney and the Ridge Meadows Hospital corridor on Laity Street, West Central is the west side of the Town Centre. The house streets between Lougheed Highway and Dewdney Trunk Road have big older lots.

entries.name: Whonnock
entries.text: Centred on Whonnock Lake and the heritage buildings along River Road, Whonnock is rural residential in eastern Maple Ridge toward the Mission border.

entries.name: Dewdney & Deroche
entries.text: Along the Lougheed Highway east of town, Dewdney and Deroche are Mission’s rural frontier. Technically they’re two unincorporated villages in FVRD Electoral Area G, not part of the City of Mission. Acreages, hobby farming and horses are the draw.

entries.name: Durieu
entries.text: A farming community in the Hatzic Valley, Durieu is Mission’s most remote rural area. Note that Durieu sits outside the City of Mission, in FVRD Electoral Area F.

entries.name: Hatzic
entries.text: Lakeside living around Hatzic Lake is what Hatzic is known for, but buyers are really choosing between two worlds: bench streets inside the City of Mission, and unincorporated Hatzic Prairie and Hatzic Island land outside it.

entries.name: Hemlock
entries.text: Hemlock is the small residential village at Sasquatch Mountain Resort, in FVRD Electoral Area C. Despite the board grouping and the mailing address, it isn’t actually in Mission.

entries.name: Lake Errock
entries.text: On its own lake near Harrison Mills, Lake Errock is a small waterfront community, and plenty of people consider it a lakeside gem. Jurisdiction-wise, it’s unincorporated land in FVRD Electoral Area C rather than part of Mission.

entries.name: Mission
entries.text: Mission sits on the north side of the Fraser and combines urban neighbourhoods with rural sub-areas. In September 2026 its medians were the lowest of the communities in its comparison group, so value is part of the story.

entries.name: Mission West
entries.text: Scenic, established hillside living on the city’s west side defines Mission West. It takes in Silverdale and the rural fringe toward Stave Falls and Ruskin, including the 3,440-acre Silverdale Comprehensive Planning Area designated for urban growth.

entries.name: Stave Falls
entries.text: Around Stave Lake, Hayward Lake and the Stave River, Stave Falls is Mission’s waterfront community, a rural area inside city limits. One thing buyers need to know: the shoreline is a BC Hydro reservoir.

entries.name: Steelhead
entries.text: Larger rural lots, forested settings and recreation toward Stave Falls and Hayward Lake make Steelhead Mission’s mountain and acreage community. It’s a separate market from the Stave Falls waterfront.

entries.name: Annieville
entries.text: Often called Delta’s oldest neighbourhood, Annieville is a quieter pocket in northwest North Delta along the Fraser River. It has big-lot character and an elementary school right in the neighbourhood.

entries.name: Beach Grove
entries.text: Shoreline lots and a golf-course edge define Beach Grove, a waterfront pocket on the Boundary Bay side of Tsawwassen, east of 56 Street.

entries.name: Boundary Beach
entries.text: At Tsawwassen’s south end on Boundary Bay, next to Boundary Bay Regional Park and running toward the border, Boundary Beach is the beachfront strip. The board sub-area is wider than the beach, though, and also takes in Southlands homes and a gated rancher community on 3 Avenue.

entries.name: Cliff Drive, Tsawwassen
entries.text: Around 12 Avenue, Cliff Drive and English Bluff Road in northwest Tsawwassen, Cliff Drive is a bluff-side pocket. The bluff and water outlook, the lot sizes and the calm streets are what people respond to. Note that it’s a Paragon sub-area name, not an official City neighbourhood.

entries.name: Delta Manor
entries.text: Around Delta Secondary School and Memorial Park, Delta Manor is the central Ladner grid. You won’t find Delta Manor on the City of Delta’s official neighbourhood list; the name comes from Paragon’s sub-areas.

entries.name: East Delta
entries.text: East of the village core, East Delta is the rural, farm side of Ladner: farmland plus the East Ladner urban edge. It isn’t a separate town or an officially named neighbourhood.

entries.name: English Bluff
entries.text: The premium end of Tsawwassen is English Bluff. Along English Bluff Road on the west shore, you’ll find large- lot waterfront and view homes on the bluff over the Strait of Georgia.

entries.name: Hawthorne
entries.text: Classic Ladner family territory, Hawthorne is a grid of detached houses anchored by Hawthorne Elementary and Hawthorne Park, with Delta Secondary for high school. Central Avenue and Ladner Trunk Road take you out to Highway 99.

entries.name: Holly
entries.text: Around Holly Elementary and Delta Secondary, Holly is an established east Ladner pocket for families. The older detached grid now has new townhomes alongside it, like Skye at Holly Park on 60B Street.

entries.name: Ladner
entries.text: Ladner is a true village community, defined by Ladner Village’s historic storefronts and Fraser River waterfront. It also takes in the Westham Island farm side and sub-areas like Hawthorne, Holly, Neilsen Grove, Delta Manor and Port Guichon.

entries.name: Ladner Elementary
entries.text: This is central Ladner, named for its school. Families target the Ladner Elementary and Delta Secondary pairing and like walking to village amenities.

entries.name: Ladner Rural
entries.text: Ladner Rural is country living on acreage: working farms, hobby farms and country homes, with much of the land in the Agricultural Land Reserve.

entries.name: Neilsen Grove, Ladner
entries.text: By the marina and golf course, Neilsen Grove (the school and the City spell it Neilson Grove) is Ladner’s riverside pocket. Hampton Cove’s townhomes and condos sit between Captain’s Cove Marina and Cove Links, with detached streets and a 55+ community nearby. Neilson Grove Elementary is on Admiral Boulevard, and the Millennium Trail runs to Deas Island Regional Park, so it’s ideal if you want a resort-style, low-maintenance Ladner lifestyle.

entries.name: Nordel
entries.text: North Delta’s civic core is Nordel, centred on the Nordel Social Heart at 84 Avenue and 112 Street, which is planned as the community focus for North Delta.

entries.name: North Delta
entries.text: Settled and mostly detached, North Delta is a community on the south bank of the Fraser. It’s made up of four sub-areas: Annieville, Nordel, Scottsdale and Sunshine Hills Woods.

check.suggested: City of Delta materials name many more than four North Delta neighbourhoods: the 2011 North Delta Area Plan set used in the City's tree-protection pilot alone lists Sunshine, Sunshine Woods, Sunshine Hills, Sunshine Village, Westview, Cougar Canyon and Scottsdale, and Delta sources also name Annieville, Nordel, Panorama Ridge, Sunbury and Canterbury Heights. Sunshine Hills and Sunshine Woods are separate neighbourhoods, not one 'Sunshine Hills Woods'.

entries.name: Port Guichon
entries.text: On River Road West, Port Guichon is historic west Ladner harbour country, the old town site and ferry-landing area.

entries.name: Scottsdale
entries.text: With Scottsdale Exchange, the R6 RapidBus and the Scott Road corridor all close at hand, Scottsdale is North Delta’s transit-friendly corner at the Surrey border.

entries.name: Sunshine Hills Woods
entries.text: The treed south end of North Delta goes by Sunshine Hills Woods. People choose it for Watershed Park and the Cougar Canyon greenbelt rather than for transit.

entries.name: Tsawwassen
entries.text: Tsawwassen is Delta’s beach community, but I think of it as several pockets: English Bluff on the bluff, Beach Grove on Boundary Bay, Pebble Hill inland and Southlands at the farm edge. Diefenbaker Park, in the middle of

entries.name: Tsawwassen Central
entries.text: Around 56 Street and 12 Avenue and the Tsawwassen Town Centre Mall, Tsawwassen Central is the heart of town.

entries.name: Tsawwassen North
entries.text: Newer strata homes and fast Highway 17 access, rather than the beach pockets, are why people choose Tsawwassen North, the newer edge by the highway.

entries.name: Central Meadows
entries.text: Along Harris Road, Central Meadows is Pitt Meadows’ civic core and Town Centre. City Hall, the rec centre, the library and Pitt Meadows Station are all here, and so are the Solaris towers at Harris and Ford, the tallest buildings in town.

entries.name: Mid Meadows
entries.text: Families like Mid Meadows for its two elementary schools, Edith McDermott and Davie Jones, plus the athletic park, the arena and the Fraser River dike trails. It’s the Bonson Road neighbourhood south of the rail line and Hammond Road, overlapping South Meadows along Bonson.

entries.name: North Meadows
entries.text: North of Lougheed Highway, Pitt Meadows splits two ways. The Highland Park and Wildwood streets near Harris Road are residential, and beyond them the rural Pitt Polder farmland and its dikes stretch toward Pitt Lake.

entries.name: Pitt Meadows
entries.text: Framed by the Pitt River, the Fraser River and farm and conservation land to the north, Pitt Meadows is a small Metro Vancouver city. It’s made up of the five Meadows sub-areas plus Osprey Village and Bonson.

entries.name: South Meadows
entries.text: Osprey Village and the South Bonson Community Centre anchor South Meadows, the South Bonson stretch of the Bonson Road corridor that runs from Hammond Road and the rail tracks down to the Fraser.

entries.name: Lower Landing
entries.text: Lower Landing is Steveston’s waterfront edge, with strata buildings and townhouses on the dyke at the south foot of No. 2 Road. It’s for buyers who’d rather have the South Dyke Trail and London’s Wharf Park at the door than a detached-house street.

check.note: NAME COLLISION: Jared's Lower Landing is in Steveston, Richmond. Our lower-landing page is Chilliwack. Held; needs a Richmond page or his decision.

entries.name: Capilano
entries.text: A canyon and mountain corridor: that’s Capilano. Buyers accept a car-oriented street on Capilano Road in exchange for the river canyon, regional park trails and the Grouse Mountain road at the door.

entries.name: Edgemont
entries.text: Established families and downsizers love Edgemont, a walkable village pocket, for the flat walk to the shops on Edgemont Boulevard.

entries.name: Altamont
entries.text: Between Dundarave village and the British Properties, with the seawalk and Marine Drive just below, Altamont is a hillside address.

entries.name: Canterbury, West Vancouver
entries.text: Views, privacy and lot size, rather than walkability, are why people choose Canterbury, a quiet British Properties enclave above Ambleside.

entries.name: Chartwell
entries.text: Schools are the centre of Chartwell, a British Properties enclave. Families buy here for the Chartwell Elementary and Sentinel Secondary pairing, both on the same drive.

entries.name: West Vancouver
entries.text: West Vancouver is a set of separate pockets rather than one market: Ambleside’s beach and seawall, Dundarave village on Marine Drive, Horseshoe Bay at the ferry terminal and the British Properties above. Each one draws a different buyer.

entries.name: Barber Street
entries.text: Waterfront and water views are the draw on Barber Street, a shoreline strip on the Port Moody Arm. The park crowds at Old Orchard Park are part of life here.

entries.name: Belcarra
entries.text: Belcarra is its own small village municipality next to Port Moody, and it feels like one. Buyers want waterfront on Belcarra Bay or a view over Bedwell Bay, and they accept the drive out Bedwell Bay Road.

entries.name: Birchland Manor
entries.text: Built around Birchland Elementary at 1331 Fraser Avenue, Birchland Manor is one of north Port Coquitlam’s smallest family pockets. The Prairie Avenue bus loop at Coast Meridian Road is on its west edge.

entries.name: Brentwood, Burnaby
entries.text: Brentwood means SkyTrain and town-centre convenience around Brentwood Town Centre. The quieter detached streets of Brentwood Park sit right beside the towers.

entries.name: Buckingham Heights
entries.text: High-end and move-up, with no strata: that’s Buckingham Heights. Buyers come for the slope above Deer Lake Park, with the cultural precinct close by.

entries.name: Burke Mountain
entries.text: In Coquitlam’s northeast growth area, Burke Mountain is a newer mountainside community where you’ll need a car. Even without SkyTrain, people choose it for newer homes, local elementary schools and trails into the provincial park.

entries.name: Burnaby
entries.text: Burnaby is a city of distinct pockets. Metrotown, Brentwood, Edmonds and the north-slope neighbourhoods all feel very different, with Deer Lake as the park heart of the older neighbourhoods.

entries.name: Burnaby Hospital Area
entries.text: The Burnaby Hospital area is a central address between Deer Lake and Metrotown. It’s especially handy for health-care workers and anyone who wants to walk to the campus.

entries.name: Burnaby Lake
entries.text: Burnaby Lake puts the lake, the trails and the sports complex at your door. Rowers, runners, birders and sports families love it, and commuters use Sperling station on the west side.

entries.name: Canyon Springs
entries.text: Right beside Coquitlam’s Town Centre, Canyon Springs is a small family pocket within walking distance of Lafarge Lake, Town Centre Park, Coquitlam Centre, Douglas College and the SkyTrain. Families look at it for Walton Elementary, home to SD43’s Mandarin bilingual program, and for Pinetree Secondary.

entries.name: Cape Horn
entries.text: Driving commuters love Cape Horn, an established detached slope with some of the quickest highway access in Coquitlam. The trade-offs are highway noise and steep grades.

entries.name: Capitol Hill
entries.text: Up on a North Burnaby hilltop with views sits Capitol Hill. Families want the schools, Confederation Park and the Hastings village, while move-up buyers chase the inlet and mountain views on the upper streets.

entries.name: Cariboo
entries.text: Cariboo ranks among Burnaby’s quieter pockets. Families buy here for the Armstrong / Cariboo Hill school pairing and the calm east-side streets rather than a town-centre address.

entries.name: Central Burnaby
entries.text: The residential side of Deer Lake is Central Burnaby, with houses and strata homes close to the park and City Hall on Canada Way nearby. It’s for buyers who want the lake without a town-centre address.

entries.name: Central Coquitlam
entries.text: Mundy Park and Como Lake Park are both close by in Central Coquitlam, an established detached neighbourhood centred on Como Lake and Austin Avenue.

entries.name: Central Park
entries.text: Near Central Park, the large forested park is at the end of the street, with two SkyTrain stations and Metrotown right beside it.

check.note: TransLink lists Patterson beside Central Park (Metrotown next along). 'Two stations right beside it' not stated.

entries.name: Central Port Coquitlam
entries.text: Downtown Port Coquitlam’s core is Central Port Coquitlam. For house buyers, the big question is how close they want to be to the West Coast Express station and the Shaughnessy Street shops.

entries.name: Chineside
entries.text: Chineside is an established detached slope that runs from Como Lake toward the Burquitlam station side, along Austin Avenue and Como Lake Avenue. Homes on the Mundy Park side often carry a premium.

entries.name: Citadel
entries.text: South of Lougheed Highway, Citadel (Citadel Heights in the City’s OCP) is an established hillside neighbourhood. Elevation, Pitt River views near Castle Park and homes backing onto green space carry a premium.

entries.name: College Park
entries.text: At Port Moody’s west edge, with Clarke Road and the Burnaby line close behind and College Park Elementary at 300 Princeton Avenue inside it, College Park is a small, settled pocket of houses. It suits buyers who want an established street over a new hillside build.

check.suggested: College Park Elementary at 300 Princeton Avenue is closed - it no longer appears among SD43's operating schools in the BC Ministry of Education school directory, so the pocket should not be described as having the school inside it.

entries.name: Connaught Heights
entries.text: Want a detached house right beside an Expo Line station? Connaught Heights is a small west-end pocket around 22nd Street Station, with a neighbourhood elementary school.

entries.name: Coquitlam
entries.text: In Coquitlam, buyers sort by pocket, school and commute, because each part of the city is its own market. The southwest side is planned around the Burquitlam and Lougheed Town Centre station areas and Austin Avenue.

entries.name: Coquitlam East
entries.text: East of Mundy Park, out toward the former Riverview lands and the Port Coquitlam side, Coquitlam East is an established detached area. Mundy Park is at one edge, and Coquitlam Central Station is the nearest rapid-transit link.

entries.name: Coquitlam West
entries.text: Coquitlam West, which the City calls Southwest Coquitlam, is built around SkyTrain. Strata buyers cluster at Burquitlam and Lougheed Town Centre, and most of Coquitlam’s condo listings are here.

entries.name: Deer Lake Place
entries.text: Prized for its Deer Lake Park and cultural-precinct setting, Deer Lake Place is a tiny enclave at the quieter west end of the lake.

entries.name: Downtown New Westminster
entries.text: New West’s riverfront downtown is Downtown New Westminster. Columbia Street is the working main street, the Westminster Pier Park boardwalk runs along the Fraser, and condo buyers go for the river-view towers at the Quay with SkyTrain overhead.

entries.name: Eagle Ridge
entries.text: Along Guildford Way and Lansdowne Drive, Eagle Ridge is an established residential bench. Families buy here for the schools, Eagle Ridge Hospital is on the same road, and City Centre is one corridor east.

entries.name: East Burnaby
entries.text: East Burnaby is a broad label. Families come for a house with a ravine or park edge and an east-side school pairing, without town-centre prices, and New Westminster commuters often buy on the Burnaby side of the line.

entries.name: Edmonds
entries.text: Some of Burnaby’s more accessible attached prices are in Edmonds, a SkyTrain town centre. The station, community centre, library branch and an urgent care clinic are all in the neighbourhood.

entries.name: Forest Glen
entries.text: Forest Glen puts attached buyers one station or one bus from Metrotown, without the Metrotown address. House buyers want the Clinton / Inman school side east of Willingdon.

entries.name: Forest Hills, Burnaby
entries.text: Staff, faculty and grad-student families make Forest Hills an SFU-connected pocket. The trails and forest of Burnaby Mountain below the university are the reason people buy here.

entries.name: Fraserview
entries.text: One of New Westminster’s lesser-known pockets, Fraserview sits by the river. Buyers weigh the river frontage and views against the Stewardson Way and bridge traffic beside it.

entries.name: Glenayre
entries.text: Young families after École Glenayre Elementary and buyers crossing from Burnaby into Port Moody are drawn to Glenayre, a small pocket.

entries.name: Glenbrooke North
entries.text: Glenbrooke North gives you the Queen’s Park-style streetscape and boulevard feel without the Queen’s Park Heritage Conservation Area permits, which don’t extend here.

entries.name: Glenwood
entries.text: Just north of Lougheed Highway, between Woodland Acres and Birchland Manor, Glenwood (which some people call Imperial Park) is a north Port Coquitlam family area. Imperial Park is the neighbourhood park, and James Park Elementary is nearby.

entries.name: Government Road
entries.text: Government Road appeals to SFU- and Lake City-connected households. They buy for the Seaforth and Stoney Creek school side and for living close to the employment corridor.

entries.name: Harbour Chines
entries.text: Most buyers simply shop Harbour Chines, a small central Coquitlam slope, as Como Lake / Central Coquitlam. Despite the name, there’s no harbour, no waterfront and no Port Coquitlam connection.

entries.name: Harbour Place, Coquitlam
entries.text: Harbour Place has a misleading name, and I always point that out. The everyday water here isn’t a harbour at all; it’s Como Lake, through Como Lake Park.

entries.name: Heritage Mountain
entries.text: Up on Port Moody’s north shore, Heritage Mountain is a hillside neighbourhood. Homes backing onto Bert Flinn Park, the views and the Heritage Mountain Elementary catchment are the draws, and City policy aims to keep its residential, forested character.

entries.name: Heritage Woods
entries.text: One of the newer neighbourhoods in the Heritage Mountain area, Heritage Woods is where families target the Aspenwood Elementary and Heritage Woods Secondary pairing.

entries.name: Highgate
entries.text: Towers by Kingsway and low-rises and townhomes on the quieter streets around Highgate Village make Highgate the Edmonds condo pocket. Edmonds Station is close, and the Byrne Creek ravine trail runs behind the blocks.

entries.name: Lincoln Park
entries.text: Between Oxford Heights and Riverwood in northeast Port Coquitlam, Lincoln Park is an established neighbourhood. Single-family houses and townhomes line its quiet streets, and Terry Fox Secondary serves the north side. With Fremont Village shopping and the Coast Meridian Overpass close by, it’s a good fit for families planning to stay put.

entries.name: Lower Mary Hill
entries.text: Houses on level lots off Pitt River Road make up Lower Mary Hill, the flat, riverside part of Mary Hill. Kilmer Park and the Traboulay PoCo Trail along the river are the local outdoors.

entries.name: Maillardville
entries.text: Coquitlam’s oldest neighbourhood is Maillardville. French-Canadian mill families settled it in 1909 around Fraser Mills, and it grew into the largest francophone community west of Manitoba. That heritage lives on in Festival du Bois, Mackin Park and the new Maillardville Community Centre, and the City’s plan to make Brunette Avenue a walkable, mixed-use village means change is coming too.

check.note: City page says 110 French Canadians arrived in 1909 and Maillardville was 'born' in June 1910; it calls it the largest Francophone centre west of Manitoba but does not call it Coquitlam's oldest neighbourhood. Needs Jared's OK on wording.

entries.name: Mary Hill
entries.text: Mostly detached homes on the hill south of downtown, with the Fraser River below, make Mary Hill Port Coquitlam’s established south side. École Mary Hill Elementary offers Early French Immersion, a big draw for families, and ƛ̓éxətəm Regional Park (formerly Colony Farm) and the river trails are close by. It suits families and value-minded buyers looking at older homes on bigger lots.

entries.name: Meadow Brook
entries.text: Meadow Brook is a small pocket in transition. Land-use-contract-era houses around Cherrybrook Place are being rezoned one parcel at a time, and Meadowbrook Elementary at 900 Sharpe Street is just south of Dewdney Trunk Road.

entries.name: Metrotown
entries.text: Metrotown is Burnaby’s town centre in the middle of a transition. Towers are rising behind the detached streets of the Maywood pockets, and people get their bearings from Metrotown Station, the bus loop and Metropolis rather than street names.

entries.name: Montecito
entries.text: Montecito appeals to families who want Montecito or Sperling elementary and the Burnaby Lake sports and park system, and to SFU-connected buyers who want to live below the mountain.

entries.name: Moody Park
entries.text: Centred on the city’s main park, Moody Park is a family neighbourhood. Buyers want a house beside the park, Lord Kelvin Elementary in the neighbourhood and the Uptown shops a few blocks east.

entries.name: Mountain Meadows
entries.text: Essentially one street on a ridge, Mountain Meadows has houses and view terraces along Noons Creek Drive and David Avenue linking the top edge to Coquitlam. It’s for buyers who want that elevated setting.

entries.name: New Horizons
entries.text: Around Nestor Street in north Coquitlam, New Horizons is a family neighbourhood with detached homes, townhomes and some condos. Many homes are within walking distance of Nestor Elementary, and Town Centre Park, Lafarge Lake and the SkyTrain are close, so you get a residential street near the Town Centre.

entries.name: New Westminster
entries.text: New Westminster is mostly attached homes, with some detached pockets. Uptown and Downtown condo buyers get some of the region’s lower attached prices, Queensborough families accept the river crossing, and Sapperton buyers tend to be tied to the hospital and the station.

entries.name: North Coquitlam
entries.text: Two places share the North Coquitlam name. The Town Centre core around Coquitlam Centre, Lafarge Lake and the Evergreen Line is full of condos and townhomes, and the quieter house streets lie north of David Avenue. Condo buyers and commuters gravitate to the core, while families looking for a house head north.

entries.name: North Shore Port Moody
entries.text: Port Moody’s north shore is mostly Pleasantside: older detached streets above and below Ioco Road, with a run of waterfront lots. Old Orchard Park has the city’s only saltwater swimming beach, the Shoreline Trail runs to Rocky Point, and Sasamat Lake and Belcarra Regional Park are just up the road. The City keeps it low-density because of Ioco Road traffic, so you get water views and an established feel.

entries.name: Oakdale
entries.text: On the Lougheed corridor, between two town-centre SkyTrain nodes (Lougheed, and Burquitlam just across the border), Oakdale is a detached Burnaby address.

entries.name: Oaklands
entries.text: Right beside Deer Lake Park on Royal Oak Avenue, Oaklands is a small low-rise pocket of mostly 1990s townhome complexes, with Royal Oak Station a short trip away. Buyers who like the lake area but want a low-rise scale tend to fit here.

entries.name: Oxford Heights
entries.text: Along the Coast Meridian corridor below Coquitlam’s Burke Mountain, Oxford Heights is an established pocket on Port Coquitlam’s north side. It’s mostly detached homes with some townhomes, many backing onto greenbelt and creek trails, and the north-side secondary is Terry Fox. Families who want a peaceful setting near trails feel at home here.

entries.name: Park Ridge Estates
entries.text: Below Burke Mountain, Park Ridge Estates is an established 1990s pocket with houses south of David Avenue backing onto the Hyde Creek greenbelt. There’s no school inside the pocket, but families choose it for the greenbelt setting.

entries.name: Port Coquitlam
entries.text: Port Coquitlam has a small-city feel, with a real downtown on Shaughnessy Street, a West Coast Express station and the Traboulay PoCo Trail looping around the city. Compared with Coquitlam and Port Moody, people choose PoCo for value, established neighbourhoods like Mary Hill, Citadel and Oxford Heights, and newer Riverwood townhomes.

entries.name: Port Moody Centre
entries.text: Built around Moody Centre and Inlet Centre stations, Port Moody Centre is the city’s walkable core on the south shore. Moody Centre is also a West Coast Express stop, with Rocky Point Park and the Brewers Row breweries on Murray Street a short walk away, while Inlet Centre is closer to Suter Brook, Newport Village and City Hall. Buyers usually pick a station first, and the Moody Centre area is planned for significant growth.

entries.name: Queen’s Park
entries.text: Prestige and heritage define Queen’s Park. Buyers love the protected streetscape beside a major city park, and they accept Heritage Alteration Permit review for exterior work.

entries.name: Queensborough
entries.text: An island community inside New Westminster: that’s Queensborough. Families accept the bridge commute in exchange for elementary and middle schools on the island, a community centre, a library branch and riverfront parks.

entries.name: Ranch Park
entries.text: If you want Mundy Park at the back fence, I point families to Ranch Park, and buyers come back to it for the big lots.

entries.name: River Springs, Coquitlam
entries.text: River Springs appeals to outdoors buyers who want the Coquitlam River Park trails, along with Burke Mountain overflow buyers and Port Coquitlam move-ups.

entries.name: Riverwood
entries.text: North of Lougheed Highway out to the Pitt River, Riverwood is Port Coquitlam’s northeast corner, built mostly in the 1980s and ’90s. It has a good mix of detached homes, townhouses and condos, with Terry Fox Secondary and Blakeburn Elementary in the area and Fremont Village and the Pitt River dike trails close by. Young families and first-time townhome buyers find a lot to like.

entries.name: Sapperton
entries.text: Defined by the hospital, Sapperton is the historic neighbourhood at New West’s northeast end. The name goes back to the Royal Engineers’ camp, “Sappers’ Town.”

entries.name: Scott Creek, Coquitlam
entries.text: Schools and a park anchor Scott Creek. Houses around Lansdowne Drive centre on Scott Creek Middle and Gleneagle Secondary at Eagle Ridge Park, with the creek corridor running through and the Coquitlam Crunch climbing above.

entries.name: Simon Fraser Hills
entries.text: Below SFU, Simon Fraser Hills is the quiet hillside, with low-rise phases stepping up from Stoney Creek toward Burnaby Mountain. It’s a fit for anyone who’d rather have the mountain setting than the North Road corridor below.

entries.name: Simon Fraser University Area
entries.text: The SFU area is a mountaintop university village. UniverCity’s townhomes and small condos sit at 366 metres beside campus, with High Street as the main street, and it draws students, staff and anyone who wants the campus and Burnaby Mountain trails at the door.

entries.name: South Slope
entries.text: Burnaby’s south-facing hill is South Slope, with houses running from Rumble Street down toward Marine Drive across the Frogger’s Creek and Byrne Creek ravines. It’s the pick for buyers who want a slope on the Royal Oak side of the city.

entries.name: Sperling-Duthie
entries.text: Move-up buyers in central Burnaby look at Sperling-Duthie. Families like the central location near Deer Lake, and high-end buyers target the Buckingham Heights view and estate properties.

entries.name: Sullivan Heights
entries.text: Older walk-ups near Cameron and townhome complexes along the Lougheed corridor make Sullivan Heights the Lougheed Town Centre condo pocket. Lougheed Station is close, and the Stoney Creek trail is a green corridor most people don’t expect beside the highway.

entries.name: Summitt View
entries.text: Still building out on the lower slope of Burke Mountain, Summitt View has townhouses, detached homes on flatter lots and view lots above David Avenue and Coast Meridian Road. Buyers are getting in while the new Burke Mountain middle and secondary schools go up off David Avenue.

entries.name: Suncrest
entries.text: Below Metrotown, Suncrest is the quiet slope, with houses running toward Marine Drive. Burnaby South Secondary at 5455 Rumble Street and Clinton Elementary at 5858 Clinton Street anchor it, so families get the schools without the towers.

entries.name: The Crest
entries.text: Within reach of Edmonds Station and the Tommy Douglas library branch, The Crest is an established East Burnaby house area with two elementary schools in the neighbourhood.

entries.name: The Heights (Massey Victory Heights), New Westminster
entries.text: Veterans-era crescents give The Heights its character as a New Westminster neighbourhood. Post-war houses and newer rebuilds line curving, tree-lined crescents, and the east-side slope looks over the rooftops to the Fraser River and Mount Baker.

entries.name: Upper Deer Lake
entries.text: Heritage-era homes near the lake’s west end and postwar homes on the upper streets by the Burnaby Village Museum make Upper Deer Lake the heritage pocket of Deer Lake. It’s the calmer, park-side alternative to Metrotown.

entries.name: Upper Eagle Ridge, Coquitlam
entries.text: Above Eagle Ridge, the upper slope holds Upper Eagle Ridge, with houses on Falcon Drive and upper Lansdowne Drive and view lots on Charter Hill Drive. Eagle Ridge Elementary is inside the pocket, and Eagle Ridge Park and the Lansdowne Drive schools are just below.

entries.name: Uptown
entries.text: Uptown is New West’s plateau neighbourhood, with houses around the Sixth Street shops and Royal City Centre, and the 2024 təməsew̓txʷ Aquatic and Community Centre as its civic anchor. People like the scale and accept that there’s no SkyTrain station on the plateau itself.

entries.name: Vancouver Heights, Burnaby
entries.text: Views define Vancouver Heights, a North Burnaby area. Families want the North Burnaby schools and Hastings Street amenities, move-up buyers want the views, and it’s popular with SFU-connected households too.

entries.name: West End
entries.text: Character houses on a slope define New West’s West End. Early-1900s homes sit beside plain post-war houses on steep streets dropping toward Fraser River views, and Twelfth Street’s heritage storefronts are the main shopping street.

check.note: Heritage inventory shows only a few early-1900s commercial buildings; most storefronts are 1920s-40s.

entries.name: Westridge
entries.text: View homes on the slope and older split-levels on the lower streets near Inlet Drive make up Westridge, Burnaby’s hillside on the inlet. Barnet Marine Park, the shoreline and the ravine trails are the draw.

entries.name: Westwood Plateau
entries.text: Built on Eagle Mountain from the late 1980s on, Westwood Plateau is a master-planned community with single- family homes, duplexes, townhouses and apartments. Westwood Plateau Village at Parkway and Johnson handles shopping, and the Westwood Plateau Golf & Country Club and Eagle Mountain trails are right there. Families come for the schools, and it’s one of Coquitlam’s go-to areas for a newer home with nature at the door.

entries.name: Willingdon Heights
entries.text: Between Hastings Street and Lougheed Highway, Willingdon Heights is a quiet pocket of interior streets, with Brentwood’s towers visible to the south and Kitchener Elementary on South Gilmore Avenue inside it. It’s the Brentwood area from a house street.

entries.name: Woodland Acres
entries.text: Mature trees line the streets of Woodland Acres, an established pocket in north Port Coquitlam on the Coquitlam border. Coquitlam Centre and the SkyTrain are minutes away, which makes it easy for families and commuters alike.
